chunks.arabic_text: رِجَالُ الْكَشِّيِّ: عَنْ حَمْدَوَيْهَ وَمُحَمَّدِ ابْنَيْ نَصِيرٍ، عَنْ مُحَمَّدِ بْنِ عِيسَى، عَنْ عَلِيِّ بْنِ الْحَكَمِ، عَنْ أَبَانَ الْأَحْمَرِ، عَنِ الطَّيَّارِ، قَالَ

translations.en: Rijal al-Kashshi: from Hamduwayh and Muhammad, the two sons of Nusayr, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban al-Ahmar, from al-Tayyar, who said:

chunks.arabic_text: قُلْتُ لِأَبِي عَبْدِ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ: بَلَغَنِي أَنَّكَ كَرِهْتَ مُنَازَرَةَ النَّاسِ، فَقَالَ: أَمَّا كَلَامُ مِثْلِكَ فَلَا يُكْرَهُ، مَنْ إِذَا طَارَ أَحْسَنَ أَنْ يَقَعَ، وَإِنْ وَقَعَ أَحْسَنَ أَنْ يَطِيرَ، فَمَنْ كَانَ هَكَذَا لَا نَكْرَهُهُ

translations.en: I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): It has been conveyed to me that you dislike debating the people. He said: As for the speech of someone like you, it is not disliked. The one who, if he flies, lands well, and if he lands, flies well — whoever is like this, we do not dislike him.

en.summary: The Imam (peace be upon him) responds to a report that he dislikes public debate by clarifying that he only dislikes it from those who lack rhetorical skill. He uses the metaphor of flying and landing to illustrate that a skilled debater can gracefully enter and exit arguments, making their participation commendable rather than disliked.
en.seo_question: What is the Imam's criterion for disliking or accepting public debate?
